To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a history of bingeing for palatable fat enhances subsequent cocaine seeking and taking in rats.

a history of binge-type intake of a palatable fatty diet enhances cocaine-seeking and - taking behaviors in rats, and that the enhanced drug-seeking and - taking is characterized by greater persistence in the face of SNA and greater effort to obtain the drug.

a history of binge-type fat intake enhances the motivation to obtain cocaine, the persistence to obtain cocaine in a situation of signaled drug nonavailability, and the effort expended to obtain cocaine.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying the neural mechanisms that underlie the development and expression of excessive behaviors toward palatable foods and substances of abuse.
understanding how excessive behavior toward one type of consummatory behavior can promote excessive behavior toward another.
the neurobiological mechanisms that underlie the loss of behavioral control over food intake, which may lead to binge eating.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results presented in this study demonstrate a relationship between binge-type intake and the development of addiction-like behaviors toward a substance.

a history of binge-type consumption of fat enhances the motivation for and persistence in seeking and taking cocaine, which is suggestive of a predisposing role for fat bingeing in the development of drug addiction.

a history of bingeing enhances the motivation for and the persistence in responding for cocaine, which is consistent with the idea that loss of control in eating disorders may predispose individuals with these disorders to loss of control over drug-taking behaviors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
binge-type eating behaviors may be an important risk factor for the development of drug addiction.
a history of bingeing enhances subsequent responding for cocaine and that this effect is mediated, at least in part, by the development of compulsive-like behaviors.
a history of bingeing enhances the motivation to take cocaine, which may be a mechanism underlying the comorbidity of bingeing and substance use disorders in humans.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the development of binge-type intake of palatable food may promote excessive behavior toward other substances of abuse.
the same factors that promote excessive behavior toward one type of reward (food) may also promote excessive behavior toward other types of rewards (drugs).
a history of binge-like eating enhances subsequent drug seeking and taking.
